title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Distinguish between populations, samples, and sub-populations
Identify appropriate distributions for different healthcare outcomes
Explain conditional vs. marginal means
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Critically interpret p-values and hypothesis tests
Recognize common pitfalls in statistical inference


This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)
\(E(Y | \text{Poor}) = \$22,619\)

Marginal mean: \(E(Y)\) - weighted average across all sub-populations

Lower than highest categories because healthier (lower-cost) people are more common!

This is a crucial concept for regression. Marginal mean averages over the distribution of X. Emphasize that weights matter.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

This retransformation issue is a major challenge in cost regression (Chapter 6). Show Table 2.2 from MEPS data.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Hypothesis Testing Framework
Purpose: Reach decision about hypothesis while quantifying error risk
Structure: - Null hypothesis \(H_0\): typically what we want to disprove - Alternative \(H_A\): what we believe - Test statistic from sample data - P-value: probability of observed data (or more extreme) if \(H_0\) is true
Decision: - Reject \(H_0\) if p-value is small - Cannot “accept” \(H_0\), only “fail to reject”

Emphasize the one-way nature. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. This asymmetry is fundamental to the framework.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
What P-values Actually Mean
P-value: Probability of observing data as or more extreme than what we saw, assuming \(H_0\) is true
Common misconception: P-value = probability that \(H_0\) is true ❌
Correct interpretation: P-value quantifies how inconsistent the data are with \(H_0\)

Low p-value → data unlikely under \(H_0\) → reject \(H_0\)
High p-value → data not inconsistent with \(H_0\) → cannot conclude anything


This is the most common misinterpretation. P-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis. Many published papers get this wrong.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Problems with P-value Thresholds
Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”
Problems:

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Effect size ≈ 0 but p < 0.001

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

5 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.23
10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Invites p-hacking: Manipulation to achieve p < 0.05


ASA statement (2016) and many journals now discourage bright-line thresholds. Focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals instead.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
section: P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
text:
P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses until finding p < 0.05
Methods: - Selective reporting of results - Choosing convenient exclusion criteria - Dichotomizing continuous variables at chosen cut-points - Dropping certain missing data patterns - Choosing specific statistical tests
Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

With large healthcare databases, this is especially tempting and problematic. Reproducibility crisis in science partly stems from this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multiple Comparisons Problem
Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05
P(at least 1 false positive) = \(1 - (0.95)^{10} = 0.40\)

Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first


In genomic studies with thousands of tests, this is critical. But even with 5-10 tests, the problem is real. Conceptual models help limit number of tests.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Best Practices for Inference
Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments
Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Key Takeaways

Healthcare outcomes require specialized distributions (not just normal)
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Conditional vs. marginal estimation is fundamental to regression
Transformation requires careful retransformation
P-values are widely misunderstood - focus on effect sizes
Standard errors matter as much as point estimates
Model assumptions affect both estimates and inference


These concepts form the foundation for regression methods in subsequent chapters. Emphasize that appropriate distribution choice is driven by outcome type.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)

text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Motivation: The Obesity Epidemic
Research Question: How has obesity prevalence changed in the US from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016?
Data: NHANES adults aged 20-59 years (n=6,864)
Key Difference from Chapter 3: - Chapter 3: Continuous BMI outcome - Chapter 4: Binary obesity indicator (BMI ≥ 30)
Why does this matter? Different question → different statistical approach

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
What Are Binary Outcomes?
Definition: Outcome Y takes one of two values

Y = 1 (positive/success/event)
Y = 0 (negative/failure/no event)

Healthcare Examples:

Hospital readmission (yes/no)
Disease presence (diabetic/not diabetic)
Treatment response (responded/did not respond)
Any medical expenditures (yes/no)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Key Property of Binary Outcomes
Critical insight:
\[E(Y) = P(Y = 1)\]
The mean of a binary outcome equals the proportion of positive outcomes
Example: If 35% of people are obese, then: - P(Obese = 1) = 0.35 - E(Obese) = 0.35
Therefore: Modeling mean = modeling proportion

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Summarizing Change: NHANES Data
Absolute change: +8% obese
But how do we express relative change?

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Relative Risk (RR)
Definition: Ratio of probabilities
\[\text{RR} = \frac{P(Y=1|X=1)}{P(Y=1|X=0)}\]
Example: \[\text{RR} = \frac{0.404}{0.325} = 1.24\]
Interpretation: 24% relative increase in obesity prevalence
When RR is useful: Intuitive for common outcomes

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Odds Ratio (OR)
Definition: Ratio of odds
\[\text{OR} = \frac{\text{Odds}(Y=1|X=1)}{\text{Odds}(Y=1|X=0)} = \frac{P(Y=1|X=1)/P(Y=0|X=1)}{P(Y=1|X=0)/P(Y=0|X=0)}\]
Example: \[\text{OR} = \frac{1899 \times 1469}{914 \times 2165} = 1.41\]
Shortcut for 2×2 tables: Product of diagonals!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
OR vs RR: Key Relationships
Three critical properties:

Direction: OR and RR always agree

Both > 1 or both < 1 or both = 1

Magnitude: OR always farther from 1 than RR

If RR = 1.24, then OR = 1.41

Rare outcomes: OR ≈ RR when outcome is rare (<10%)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
section: When OR ≠ RR: A Cautionary Tale
text:
When OR ≠ RR: A Cautionary Tale
Critical point: With common outcomes (like obesity at ~35%), OR can be misleading if interpreted as RR
Famous example: 1999 NEJM cardiac catheterization study - OR = 0.60 (seemed dramatic) - RR = 0.93 (actually modest)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Can We Use Linear Regression?
Technically yes, but…
Three major problems:

Predictions can be < 0 or > 1
Binary outcomes aren’t normally distributed
Variance isn’t constant across X values

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Problem 1: Impossible Predictions
Linear regression doesn’t respect [0,1] bounds
Example predictions: - Age 20: -0.12 → Negative probability! ❌ - Age 90: 1.31 → Probability > 1! ❌
What we need: Model that always produces values in [0, 1]

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Linear vs Logistic: Visual Comparison
![Comparison showing linear regression can go outside [0,1] bounds while logistic stays within]
Key observation: - Linear: straight line (can exceed bounds) - Logistic: S-shaped curve (always between 0 and 1)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
The Logistic Transformation
Goal: Transform linear combination to stay in [0, 1]
Solution: Use the logistic function
\[P(Y_i = 1) = \frac{\exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ki})}{1 + \exp(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ki})}\]
Why this works: - As \(\beta_0 + \beta X \to +\infty\), P(Y=1) → 1 - As \(\beta_0 + \beta X \to -\infty\), P(Y=1) → 0 - Numerator always < denominator

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Alternative Formulation: The Logit
Equivalent formulation (keeps linearity on transformed scale):
\[\log\left[\frac{P(Y_i=1)}{P(Y_i=0)}\right] = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{1i} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ki}\]
Key insight: We model the log odds (logit) as a linear function
Important terms: - Odds = P(Y=1) / P(Y=0) - Logit = log(odds) - Logistic function = inverse of logit

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Why the Logit?
Advantages of modeling log(odds):

Range: Odds can be any positive number
Log of odds: Can be any real number (-∞ to +∞)
Multiplicative interpretation: Natural for odds ratios

Mathematical connection:
\[\text{If } \log(\text{odds}) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X\]
\[\text{Then } \text{OR} = \exp(\beta_1)\]

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Estimation: Maximum Likelihood
Key difference from linear regression:

Linear regression: Minimize sum of squared errors
Logistic regression: Maximize likelihood

What is likelihood? - Probability of observing the data given parameters - Choose β values that make observed data most probable
Good news: When outcome is normal, maximum likelihood = least squares!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Example: Simple Model
How do we interpret these numbers?

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Interpretation on Log Odds Scale
Coefficient = 0.343
Interpretation: The log odds of being obese increased by 0.343 from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016
Problem: What does “log odds of 0.343” mean? 🤔
Solution: Exponentiate to get odds ratio!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Interpretation on Odds Scale
Odds Ratio: \[\text{OR} = \exp(0.343) = 1.41\]
Interpretation: The odds of being obese in 2015-2016 were 1.41 times the odds in 1999-2000
Slightly better, but… - What does “1.41 times the odds” mean? - Most people think in probabilities, not odds!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Calculating Probabilities
We can calculate predicted probabilities for specific groups:
1999-2000: \[P(\text{Obese}) = \frac{\exp(-0.731)}{1 + \exp(-0.731)} = 0.325\]
2015-2016: \[P(\text{Obese}) = \frac{\exp(-0.731 + 0.343)}{1 + \exp(-0.731 + 0.343)} = 0.404\]
These match our two-way table exactly!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Multivariate Model: NHANES
How do we interpret these?

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Interpreting Categorical Predictors
SEX = Female: OR = 1.48
Correct interpretation: Women have 1.48 times the odds of being obese compared to men, holding all other variables constant
What “holding constant” means: This OR is the same for: - 25-year-old Non-Hispanic White in 1999-2000 - 50-year-old Mexican American in 2015-2016 - Any combination of other covariates

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Interpreting Continuous Predictors
AGE: Coefficient = 0.02, OR = 1.02
Interpretation: Each additional year of age is associated with 1.02 times the odds of being obese
For larger changes: - 10 years: OR = exp(0.02 × 10) = exp(0.2) = 1.22 - 20 years: OR = exp(0.02 × 20) = exp(0.4) = 1.49
Remember: Effect is the same at ANY starting age (linearity assumption)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Common Pitfall: OR ≠ RR
Wrong interpretation: ❌ “Women are 48% more likely to be obese”
Why wrong? - OR = 1.48 means 48% increase in odds, not probability - With common outcomes, OR overstates the effect
Correct interpretation: ✓ “Women have 48% higher odds of obesity”
Better yet: Calculate effect on probability scale (coming next!)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
The Problem
What we have: - Effects on log odds scale (hard to interpret) - Effects on odds scale (better, but not intuitive)
What we want: - Effects on probability scale (intuitive!)
The challenge: Effects depend on values of OTHER covariates 😟

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
section: Why Effects Depend on Other Covariates
text:
Why Effects Depend on Other Covariates
![Graph showing predicted probabilities by age, sex, and year]
Observations: - Effect of YEAR varies by AGE and SEX - Absolute change larger for older people - Relative change larger for younger people - Only OR is constant!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Solution: Marginal Effects
Idea: Average the conditional effects across the population
Marginal Additive Effect: 1. For each person, calculate: P(Y=1|X=1) - P(Y=1|X=0) 2. Average these differences across all people
Result: Single number representing average change in probability

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Recycled Predictions Method
Step-by-step process:

Fit logistic regression with all covariates
For each person in data:

Set X to value 1, calculate predicted P(Y=1)
Set X to value 0, calculate predicted P(Y=1)
Take difference

Average all differences
Get standard error (using delta method or bootstrap)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Example: Effect of Year
Marginal additive effect = 0.102 (95% CI: 0.077, 0.128)
Interpretation: The probability of being obese increased by about 10 percentage points from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016
Compare to: - OR = 1.55 (55% increase in odds) - Linear regression coefficient ≈ 0.098 (very close!)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Marginal Effects: Key Points
Advantages: - Intuitive interpretation (probability scale) - Single number summary - Adjusted for all covariates
Limitations: - Depends on distribution of covariates in sample - May not generalize if sample not representative - Not actually “causal” (despite terminology)
Implementation: Use margins package in R

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Three Types of Model Evaluation
Your objective determines evaluation criteria:

Hypothesis testing: Are assumptions satisfied?
Causal inference: Are confounders controlled?
Prediction: How accurate are predictions?

Different objectives → different evaluation methods

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Comparing Models: Likelihood Ratio Test
For nested models:

Restricted model: Excludes some variables
Full model: Includes all variables

Test statistic: \[-2[\log L_{\text{restricted}} - \log L_{\text{full}}]\]
Compare to χ² distribution
Example: Testing if RACE matters (4 additional parameters)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Comparing Models: AIC and BIC
For any models (nested or not):
\[\text{AIC} = -2\log L + 2k\] \[\text{BIC} = -2\log L + k\log(n)\]
where k = number of parameters, n = sample size
Interpretation: Lower is better
Difference: - AIC: More lenient about complexity - BIC: Penalizes complexity more heavily

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Model Calibration: Hosmer-Lemeshow
Purpose: Check if predicted probabilities match observed frequencies
Method: 1. Order observations by predicted probability 2. Split into m groups (usually 10) 3. Compare observed vs. expected counts in each group 4. Calculate χ² statistic
Interpretation: - Low p-value → poor calibration - BUT: Very sensitive with large n - Better used informally to identify patterns

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Example: H-L Test Results
Pearson residual = (Observed - Predicted) / √Predicted
Look for: Systematic patterns or extreme residuals

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
From Probabilities to Classifications
Logistic regression gives: P(Y=1) ∈ [0,1]
Often need: Binary prediction (0 or 1)
Solution: Choose threshold T - If P(Y=1) > T → predict Y=1 - If P(Y=1) ≤ T → predict Y=0
Common choice: T = 0.5

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
The 2×2 Classification Table
Four outcomes: - True Negative (TN): Correctly predict negative - True Positive (TP): Correctly predict positive - False Positive (FP): Incorrectly predict positive (Type I error) - False Negative (FN): Incorrectly predict negative (Type II error)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Key Performance Metrics
Sensitivity (True Positive Rate): \[\text{Sensitivity} = \frac{TP}{TP + FN}\] Proportion of actual positives correctly identified
Specificity (True Negative Rate): \[\text{Specificity} = \frac{TN}{TN + FP}\] Proportion of actual negatives correctly identified
Trade-off: As threshold ↑, sensitivity ↓ but specificity ↑

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Example: Obesity Predictions (T=0.5)
Results: - Sensitivity = 18.2% (poor!) - Specificity = 92.0% (good)
Why imbalanced? Default threshold may not be optimal

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
ROC Curve: Threshold-Free Evaluation
Receiver Operating Characteristic (ROC) curve:

X-axis: False Positive Rate (1 - Specificity)
Y-axis: True Positive Rate (Sensitivity)
Plot for ALL possible thresholds

Interpretation: - Perfect model: Hugs upper-left corner - Random guessing: 45-degree line - Better model: Curve above 45-degree line

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Area Under the Curve (AUC)
Definition: Area under ROC curve
Interpretation: - AUC = 1.0: Perfect predictions - AUC = 0.5: Random guessing - AUC = 0.7: Decent - AUC = 0.9: Excellent
Obesity example: AUC = 0.63 - Modest predictive power - Could improve with more/better predictors

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Clinical Context Matters
Example: COVID-19 Testing
Diagnostic test (active infection): - Priority: High sensitivity - Why: False negatives spread infection
Antibody test (past infection): - Priority: High specificity - Why: False positives lead to risky behavior
Lesson: Optimal threshold depends on consequences of errors

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Extension to >2 Categories
When to use: Outcome has multiple categories
BMI Example: 4 categories - Underweight (BMI < 18.5) - Normal (18.5 ≤ BMI < 25) - Overweight (25 ≤ BMI < 30) - Obese (BMI ≥ 30)
Question: How did distribution across categories change from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016?

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Two-Way Table: BMI Categories
Observations: - Large increase in obese - Decrease in normal and overweight - Little change in underweight

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Multinomial Logistic Regression
Key idea: Run K-1 logistic regressions
For K=4 categories with “normal” as reference:
\[\log\left(\frac{P(Y=\text{underweight})}{P(Y=\text{normal})}\right) = \beta_0 + \beta_1X\]
\[\log\left(\frac{P(Y=\text{overweight})}{P(Y=\text{normal})}\right) = \gamma_0 + \gamma_1X\]
\[\log\left(\frac{P(Y=\text{obese})}{P(Y=\text{normal})}\right) = \delta_0 + \delta_1X\]
Each equation: Separate set of coefficients!

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Multi-Category Odds Ratios
Definition: \[\text{OR}_k = \frac{P(Y=k|X=1)/P(Y=\text{ref}|X=1)}{P(Y=k|X=0)/P(Y=\text{ref}|X=0)}\]
Example results for YEAR: - Underweight: OR = 1.16 - Overweight: OR = 1.18 - Obese: OR = 1.69
Interpretation: Shift from normal category into each non-normal category

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Separate Logistic vs. Multinomial
Two approaches:

Separate: Fit each category vs. reference separately
Joint: Fit multinomial model

Result: Nearly identical coefficients!
Why joint is better: - More efficient - Predictions across categories sum to 1 - Can test overall effect of predictor

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Multinomial Results: Interpretation
YEAR = 2015-2016 coefficients: Interpretation: From 1999-2000 to 2015-2016: - 16% increase in odds of underweight vs. normal - 18% increase in odds of overweight vs. normal
- 69% increase in odds of obese vs. normal

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Marginal Effects for Multinomial
Same recycled predictions approach:

Calculate predicted probabilities for each category
Set covariate to each value
Take differences
Average across sample

Result: Change in probability for each category

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Marginal Effects: BMI Example
Interpretation: - 7% decrease in probability of normal weight - 10% increase in probability of obese - Probabilities sum to 0 (as they must!)

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Ordered Logistic Regression
Proportional odds model: Assumes ordered categories
Structure: \[\logit[P(Y > k)] = \gamma_k + \beta X\]
Single coefficient β describes effect on ALL thresholds
Strong assumption: Effect is monotone across categories
Problem: Often unrealistic - Example: Both underweight AND obese increase with age in elderly
Recommendation: Use unordered multinomial unless specific hypothesis warrants ordered model

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Critical Distinctions
Odds vs. Probability: - Odds = P(Y=1) / P(Y=0) - Probability = P(Y=1) - They’re different! (except when P(Y=1) is small)
OR vs. RR: - Both measure association - OR always farther from 1 - OR ≈ RR only when outcome is rare
Conditional vs. Marginal: - Conditional: Effect at specific covariate values - Marginal: Average effect across population

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Why Not Linear Regression?
Three reasons:

Can predict impossible probabilities (<0 or >1)
Binary outcomes aren’t normally distributed
Variance not constant

Solution: Logistic regression using logit link

title: Lecture 9: Logistic Regression Analysis
text:
Interpretation Hierarchy
Three levels of interpretation:

Log odds: β coefficients

Hard to interpret directly

Odds: exp(β) = OR

Better, but still not intuitive
Only measure that doesn’t depend on other covariates

Probability: Marginal effects

Most intuitive
Depends on covariate distribution in sample

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Distinguish between populations, samples, and sub-populations
Identify appropriate distributions for different healthcare outcomes
Explain conditional vs. marginal means
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Critically interpret p-values and hypothesis tests
Recognize common pitfalls in statistical inference


This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)
\(E(Y | \text{Poor}) = \$22,619\)

Marginal mean: \(E(Y)\) - weighted average across all sub-populations
\[E(Y) = 1957(0.34) + 3729(0.29) + 6183(0.25) + 11387(0.10) + 22619(0.03)\] \[= \$5,110\]
Lower than highest categories because healthier (lower-cost) people are more common!

This is a crucial concept for regression. Marginal mean averages over the distribution of X. Emphasize that weights matter.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

This retransformation issue is a major challenge in cost regression (Chapter 6). Show Table 2.2 from MEPS data.

Lognormal Distribution

Right-skewed with heavy right tail, suitable for expenditure data

Different σ values control the degree of skewness. Larger σ → heavier tail.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Hypothesis Testing Framework
Purpose: Reach decision about hypothesis while quantifying error risk
Structure: - Null hypothesis \(H_0\): typically what we want to disprove - Alternative \(H_A\): what we believe - Test statistic from sample data - P-value: probability of observed data (or more extreme) if \(H_0\) is true
Decision: - Reject \(H_0\) if p-value is small - Cannot “accept” \(H_0\), only “fail to reject”

Emphasize the one-way nature. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. This asymmetry is fundamental to the framework.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
What P-values Actually Mean
P-value: Probability of observing data as or more extreme than what we saw, assuming \(H_0\) is true
Common misconception: P-value = probability that \(H_0\) is true ❌
Correct interpretation: P-value quantifies how inconsistent the data are with \(H_0\)

Low p-value → data unlikely under \(H_0\) → reject \(H_0\)
High p-value → data not inconsistent with \(H_0\) → cannot conclude anything


This is the most common misinterpretation. P-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis. Many published papers get this wrong.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Problems with P-value Thresholds
Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”
Problems:

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Effect size ≈ 0 but p < 0.001

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

5 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.23
10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Invites p-hacking: Manipulation to achieve p < 0.05


ASA statement (2016) and many journals now discourage bright-line thresholds. Focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals instead.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
section: P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
text:
P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses until finding p < 0.05
Methods: - Selective reporting of results - Choosing convenient exclusion criteria - Dichotomizing continuous variables at chosen cut-points - Dropping certain missing data patterns - Choosing specific statistical tests
Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

With large healthcare databases, this is especially tempting and problematic. Reproducibility crisis in science partly stems from this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multiple Comparisons Problem
Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05
P(at least 1 false positive) = \(1 - (0.95)^{10} = 0.40\)

Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first


In genomic studies with thousands of tests, this is critical. But even with 5-10 tests, the problem is real. Conceptual models help limit number of tests.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Best Practices for Inference
Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments
Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Key Takeaways

Healthcare outcomes require specialized distributions (not just normal)
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Conditional vs. marginal estimation is fundamental to regression
Transformation requires careful retransformation
P-values are widely misunderstood - focus on effect sizes
Standard errors matter as much as point estimates
Model assumptions affect both estimates and inference


These concepts form the foundation for regression methods in subsequent chapters. Emphasize that appropriate distribution choice is driven by outcome type.

Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:

Each test at α = 0.05

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:

Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments

text:
Best Practices for Inference
Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments
Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Key Takeaways

Healthcare outcomes require specialized distributions (not just normal)
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Conditional vs. marginal estimation is fundamental to regression
Transformation requires careful retransformation
P-values are widely misunderstood - focus on effect sizes
Standard errors matter as much as point estimates
Model assumptions affect both estimates and inference


These concepts form the foundation for regression methods in subsequent chapters. Emphasize that appropriate distribution choice is driven by outcome type.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Distinguish between populations, samples, and sub-populations
Identify appropriate distributions for different healthcare outcomes
Explain conditional vs. marginal means
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Critically interpret p-values and hypothesis tests
Recognize common pitfalls in statistical inference


This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

This table illustrates both conditional and marginal means. Each expenditure is conditional on health status.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)
\(E(Y | \text{Poor}) = \$22,619\)

Marginal mean: \(E(Y)\) - weighted average across all sub-populations
\[E(Y) = 1957(0.34) + 3729(0.29) + 6183(0.25) + 11387(0.10) + 22619(0.03)\] \[= \$5,110\]
Lower than highest categories because healthier (lower-cost) people are more common!

This is a crucial concept for regression. Marginal mean averages over the distribution of X. Emphasize that weights matter.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

This retransformation issue is a major challenge in cost regression (Chapter 6). Show Table 2.2 from MEPS data.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution

Right-skewed with heavy right tail, suitable for expenditure data

Different σ values control the degree of skewness. Larger σ → heavier tail.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Hypothesis Testing Framework
Purpose: Reach decision about hypothesis while quantifying error risk
Structure: - Null hypothesis \(H_0\): typically what we want to disprove - Alternative \(H_A\): what we believe - Test statistic from sample data - P-value: probability of observed data (or more extreme) if \(H_0\) is true
Decision: - Reject \(H_0\) if p-value is small - Cannot “accept” \(H_0\), only “fail to reject”

Emphasize the one-way nature. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. This asymmetry is fundamental to the framework.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
What P-values Actually Mean
P-value: Probability of observing data as or more extreme than what we saw, assuming \(H_0\) is true
Common misconception: P-value = probability that \(H_0\) is true ❌
Correct interpretation: P-value quantifies how inconsistent the data are with \(H_0\)

Low p-value → data unlikely under \(H_0\) → reject \(H_0\)
High p-value → data not inconsistent with \(H_0\) → cannot conclude anything


This is the most common misinterpretation. P-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis. Many published papers get this wrong.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Problems with P-value Thresholds
Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”
Problems:

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Effect size ≈ 0 but p < 0.001

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

5 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.23
10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Invites p-hacking: Manipulation to achieve p < 0.05


ASA statement (2016) and many journals now discourage bright-line thresholds. Focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals instead.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
section: P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
text:
P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses until finding p < 0.05
Methods: - Selective reporting of results - Choosing convenient exclusion criteria - Dichotomizing continuous variables at chosen cut-points - Dropping certain missing data patterns - Choosing specific statistical tests
Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

With large healthcare databases, this is especially tempting and problematic. Reproducibility crisis in science partly stems from this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multiple Comparisons Problem
Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05
P(at least 1 false positive) = \(1 - (0.95)^{10} = 0.40\)

Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first


In genomic studies with thousands of tests, this is critical. But even with 5-10 tests, the problem is real. Conceptual models help limit number of tests.

Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis

Why Survey Methods Matter


The Problem:

Health surveys rarely use simple random sampling
Ignoring survey design → incorrect standard errors
Wrong inference → poor policy decisions


Real Example:

NHIS 2015: New diabetes cases declining
1.7M (2009) → 1.4M (2014)
How reliable are these estimates?

Three Major Health Surveys








Survey
Focus
Design

MEPS
