title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Common Survey Biases
Three critical threats to validity:

Non-response bias: Systematically different responders

Example: Satisfaction surveys over-represent dissatisfied patients

Recall bias: Memory linked to outcome

Cancer recurrence cases may recall treatment details better

Social desirability bias: Under-reporting sensitive behaviors

Alcohol use, medication adherence, mask-wearing








Warning


Survey design and question validation are crucial mitigation strategies

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
What is Stratification?
Definition: Partition population into predetermined subgroups (strata), sample independently from each
Two main objectives:

Control sample composition
Reduce variability in results

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Stratification Example


NHIS Strategy:

Geographic strata (states)
Demographic strata
Until 2016: oversampled minorities
2016+: oversampled 10 least populous states


Why?

Ensure rural areas represented
Sufficient minority samples
Enable subgroup analyses
Improve precision

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Stratification and Variance Reduction
Consider self-reported health stratified by age:

Health status declines with age (between-strata heterogeneity)
Within age groups, more similar responses (within-strata homogeneity)
Fixed sampling fractions per stratum → predictable composition
Result: Lower variance than simple random sampling

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Mathematical Insight
For stratified design with \(K\) strata:
\[\text{Var}_{\text{stratified}} = \sum_{i=1}^{K} W_i^2 \sigma_i^2\]
where:

\(W_i\) = stratum weight (relative size)
\(\sigma_i^2\) = within-stratum variance







Tip


When strata are homogeneous within and heterogeneous between, variance is smaller than simple random sampling

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
What is Clustering?
Definition: Sample groups (clusters) together for convenience and cost-efficiency
Key difference from stratification:



Stratification
Clustering




All strata represented
Not all clusters sampled


Known in advance which strata
Random which clusters


Reduces variance
Increases variance

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Clustering Example
NHIS Two-Stage Design:

Primary Sampling Units (PSUs): Geographic regions (~400 from ~1900)
Secondary Sampling Units (SSUs): Households within PSUs

Why cluster?

In-person interviews → must cluster by location
Cost efficiency vs. statistical efficiency tradeoff

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Why Clustering Increases Variance


Intuition:

Individuals in same cluster are similar
Not as much information as independent samples
Must account for within-cluster correlation


Extreme Example:

Flu shot survey by families
All family members same behavior
100 people = only 25 independent observations

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Variance Components
For clustered design:
\[\text{Var}_{\text{total}} = \text{Var}_{\text{between-cluster}} + \text{Var}_{\text{within-cluster}}\]






Warning


Single-stage clustering: Only between-cluster variance matters (within-cluster variance = 0 if all sampled)
Two-stage clustering: Both sources contribute

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Why Weights?
The fundamental issue:

Stratified designs with oversampling are not population-representative
Need to reconstruct population composition
Use weights = inverse of sampling probabilities

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis

Understanding Weights
Each weight represents: Number of population individuals represented by one sample observation
Example (Maternal & Infant Health Survey):

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
Post-Stratification
The problem: Non-response disrupts planned sampling fractions
The solution: Adjust weights based on observed response rates
Example:

Planned: 320 respondents age <25
Actual: 256 respondents (80% response)
Post-stratification multiplier: 5/4 = 1.25

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis

Raking
When: Multiple stratification variables
What: Iteratively adjust weights so weighted sample matches population on each margin
Example: Maternal & Infant Health Survey - 6 strata: race (2 levels) × birthweight (3 levels) - Raking ensures marginal distributions correct for both race and birthweight

title: Lecture 5: Healthcare Survey Data Analysis
text:
The Challenge
Standard errors must account for:

Stratification (reduces variance)
Clustering (increases variance)

Weights (random, data-dependent)

Key principle:

“Variance measures fluctuation if survey repeated many times in same population”

1. Linearization (Delta Method)

Mathematical approximation
Taylor series expansion

Computationally efficient


2. Replication Methods

Create multiple replicate datasets

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

Distinguish between populations, samples, and sub-populations
Identify appropriate distributions for different healthcare outcomes
Explain conditional vs. marginal means
Understand overdispersion and between-individual heterogeneity
Critically interpret p-values and hypothesis tests
Recognize common pitfalls in statistical inference


This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Conditional vs. Marginal Means (cont.)
Conditional mean: \(E(Y | X = x)\) - mean for specific sub-population

\(E(Y | \text{Excellent}) = \$1,957\)
\(E(Y | \text{Poor}) = \$22,619\)

Marginal mean: \(E(Y)\) - weighted average across all sub-populations
\[E(Y) = 1957(0.34) + 3729(0.29) + 6183(0.25) + 11387(0.10) + 22619(0.03)\] \[= \$5,110\]
Lower than highest categories because healthier (lower-cost) people are more common!

This is a crucial concept for regression. Marginal mean averages over the distribution of X. Emphasize that weights matter.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Bernoulli and Binomial Distributions
Bernoulli: Binary outcome (0 or 1)

Parameter: \(p = P(Y = 1)\)
Mean: \(E(Y) = p\)
Variance: \(Var(Y) = p(1-p)\)
Variance depends on mean!

Binomial: Sum of n independent Bernoulli variables

Parameters: n (number of trials), p (success probability)
Mean: \(np\)
Variance: \(np(1-p)\)

Example: Hospital re-admissions after surgery

Binary prediction is a classification problem. Statistical learning has different algorithms for this (Chapter 10). Emphasize that binomial requires independence - clustering violates this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Binomial Distribution

Shape depends on both n and p. As n increases, distribution becomes more bell-shaped.

Show how the distribution changes with parameters. When p=0.5 and n is large, it approaches normal distribution (Central Limit Theorem preview).

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multinomial Distribution
Generalization of binomial for multiple categories (K > 2)
Examples:

Treatment choice: surgery/radiation/hormonal (3 unordered categories)
Health status: excellent/very good/good/fair/poor (5 ordered categories)

Parameters: K-1 independent probabilities (must sum to 1)
Analysis Goal: Identify factors predicting probability of each category

How does diabetes affect \(P(Y = k)\) for each health status category k?


Ordered vs. unordered categories require different modeling approaches. Can treat ordered as continuous or use ordinal regression methods.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution for Counts
Basic distribution for count data (0, 1, 2, 3, …)
Assumptions: - Events occur at constant rate - Memoryless (past doesn’t affect future probability)
Parameter: λ (mean rate)
Key property: Mean = Variance = λ
Highly restrictive for healthcare data!

Show Figure 2.3. The equal mean-variance assumption is almost always violated in practice. Healthcare counts typically show overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Poisson Distribution


As λ increases, distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Overdispersion in Healthcare Data

Observed MEPS outpatient visits vs. Simulated Poisson

Observed: Mean = 1.5, Variance = 24 (16× mean!)
More zeros and longer right tail than Poisson predicts


This is typical of healthcare utilization data. Poisson assumption is too restrictive. Need alternative models.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Negative Binomial Distribution
Accommodates overdispersion: Variance > Mean
Mechanism: Between-individual heterogeneity

Each person has their own latent “frailty” or “susceptibility”
Some rarely seek care (low frailty), others frequently (high frailty)
Individual’s conditional mean: \(\mu r_i\) (where \(r_i\) is personal frailty)

Result: If frailties follow gamma distribution with mean 1, variance α - Marginal distribution of Y is negative binomial - Mean: μ - Variance: \(\mu(1 + \alpha\mu)\) > \(\mu\)

This latent heterogeneity concept recurs in random effects and frailty models. Emphasize that it’s a specific mechanism for overdispersion.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution
Symmetric, bell-shaped distribution
Parameters: mean μ, standard deviation σ
Key properties: - 67% of observations within 1 SD of mean - 95% within 2 SDs - Values >2 SDs away are “atypical”
Standardization: \(Z = (Y - \mu)/\sigma\) has mean 0, SD 1

Show Figure 2.5. Most healthcare outcomes are NOT normal, but the normal is crucial because of the Central Limit Theorem - sample means are approximately normal.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Normal Distribution


Different σ values show different spreads. The distribution is completely determined by μ and σ.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Central Limit Theorem
Key insight: Even if data are non-normal, sample means are approximately normal

Distribution of sample mean \(\bar{Y}\) approaches normal as n increases
True regardless of the distribution of Y itself
Enables hypothesis testing based on normal approximation

Crucial distinction: - Population data distribution: Often non-normal in healthcare - Sample estimate distribution: Approximately normal

This is why we can use normal-based inference even with skewed healthcare data. But this applies to the sampling distribution of estimates, not the data itself.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution
Flexible distribution for non-negative, continuous, right-skewed outcomes
Parameters: α (shape), β (rate)

Mean: α/β
Variance: α/β²

Can accommodate various shapes from highly skewed to more symmetric
Commonly used for medical expenditures

Show Figure 2.6. The gamma is quite flexible and can match many right-skewed distributions. The variance can be greater or less than the mean.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Gamma Distribution


As α increases (for fixed β), the distribution becomes more symmetric and bell-shaped.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution
Y has lognormal distribution if log(Y) has normal distribution
If \(\log(Y) \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)\), then:
\[E(Y) = \exp\left(\mu + \frac{1}{2}\sigma^2\right) \neq \exp(\mu)\]
Critical point: Order of operations matters!

\(E[\log(Y)] \neq \log[E(Y)]\)
Retransformation is not straightforward

Usage: Any log-transformed regression implicitly assumes lognormal outcomes

This retransformation issue is a major challenge in cost regression (Chapter 6). Show Table 2.2 from MEPS data.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Lognormal Distribution

Right-skewed with heavy right tail, suitable for expenditure data

Different σ values control the degree of skewness. Larger σ → heavier tail.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Hypothesis Testing Framework
Purpose: Reach decision about hypothesis while quantifying error risk
Structure: - Null hypothesis \(H_0\): typically what we want to disprove - Alternative \(H_A\): what we believe - Test statistic from sample data - P-value: probability of observed data (or more extreme) if \(H_0\) is true
Decision: - Reject \(H_0\) if p-value is small - Cannot “accept” \(H_0\), only “fail to reject”

Emphasize the one-way nature. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence. This asymmetry is fundamental to the framework.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
What P-values Actually Mean
P-value: Probability of observing data as or more extreme than what we saw, assuming \(H_0\) is true
Common misconception: P-value = probability that \(H_0\) is true ❌
Correct interpretation: P-value quantifies how inconsistent the data are with \(H_0\)

Low p-value → data unlikely under \(H_0\) → reject \(H_0\)
High p-value → data not inconsistent with \(H_0\) → cannot conclude anything


This is the most common misinterpretation. P-value is a statement about the data, not about the hypothesis. Many published papers get this wrong.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Problems with P-value Thresholds
Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”
Problems:

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Effect size ≈ 0 but p < 0.001

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

5 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.23
10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Invites p-hacking: Manipulation to achieve p < 0.05


ASA statement (2016) and many journals now discourage bright-line thresholds. Focus on effect sizes and confidence intervals instead.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
section: P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
text:
P-hacking and Researcher Degrees of Freedom
P-hacking: Trying multiple analyses until finding p < 0.05
Methods: - Selective reporting of results - Choosing convenient exclusion criteria - Dichotomizing continuous variables at chosen cut-points - Dropping certain missing data patterns - Choosing specific statistical tests
Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

With large healthcare databases, this is especially tempting and problematic. Reproducibility crisis in science partly stems from this.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Multiple Comparisons Problem
Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05
P(at least 1 false positive) = \(1 - (0.95)^{10} = 0.40\)

Solutions:

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first


In genomic studies with thousands of tests, this is critical. But even with 5-10 tests, the problem is real. Conceptual models help limit number of tests.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Best Practices for Inference
Do: - Report effect sizes with confidence intervals - Consider practical significance alongside statistical significance - Acknowledge uncertainty in p-values themselves - Pre-specify hypotheses when possible - Report all analyses conducted - Consider multiple comparison adjustments
Don’t: - Treat p = 0.049 differently from p = 0.051 - Conclude \(H_0\) is true from large p-value - Interpret p-value as P(\(H_0\) is true) - Hide analyses that didn’t achieve p < 0.05

Growing recognition in scientific community of these limitations. Many journals now require pre-registration of analysis plans. Emphasize reproducibility.

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you will be able to:

Explain four distinct perspectives of regression analysis
Interpret regression coefficients correctly
Understand confounding and effect modification
Apply model selection techniques appropriately
Assess model assumptions and goodness of fit

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Course Context
Data Source: NHANES (National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey)
Research Question: How has BMI changed in the US from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016?
Population: Adults aged 20-59 years

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
1. Quantifying Association


Purpose: - Summarize relationship between X and Y - One-number summary of how E(Y) changes with X
Key Point: - Association ≠ Causation in observational studies

Example: - How does BMI change per year of age? - Coefficient β₁ = 0.07 - Interpretation: BMI increases by 0.07 units per year of age

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
2. Explaining Variability
Core Question: How much of the variability in Y is due to X?

Left panel: Variability around overall mean E(Y)
Right panel: Variability around E(Y|X)

Key Metric: R² (coefficient of determination)

R² = 0.70 means 70% of variance explained
Use adjusted R² when comparing models

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
3. Estimating Intervention Effects


Focus on causal effects
Key Challenge: - Observational data ≠ experimental data - Cannot simply interpret β as causal
Requirements: - Control for confounders - Special methods (Chapter 8)

Example: Physical exercise and BMI

Simple model: β = -2.15
Adjusted for age: β = -1.88
Difference due to confounding

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
4. Predicting Outcomes
Goal: Accurate prediction of future Y values
Key Differences from other perspectives:

Focus on predictive accuracy, not explanation
May include many variables without scientific rationale
Different evaluation criteria
Hypothesis testing not appropriate after data-driven selection

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Basic Model Structure
For individual i:
\[Y_i = \beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ik} + \epsilon_i\]
Two parts:

Systematic part: \(\beta_0 + \beta_1X_{i1} + \cdots + \beta_kX_{ik}\)
Random part: \(\epsilon_i\)

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Model Assumptions
About the systematic part:

Linearity: One-unit change in X → constant change in E(Y)
Additivity: Effects of Xs combine additively

About the random part (ε):

Normal distribution with mean zero
Constant variance across all sub-populations
Independence between observations

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Which Assumptions Matter When?


For valid β estimates: - Correct systematic part - That’s it!
For valid standard errors: - All three assumptions about random part

Important: - Estimates are unbiased even if ε not normal - But SEs, CIs, and p-values may be wrong - Large samples help with normality

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Least Squares
Objective: Minimize sum of squared differences
\[\text{Minimize: } \sum_{i=1}^n (Y_i - \hat{Y}_i)^2\]
Properties:

Does NOT require distributional assumptions
Simple computational solution
Finds the “closest” line to observed data

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Maximum Likelihood
Objective: Find β values that maximize probability of observing the data
Properties:

Requires distributional assumptions (normal for linear regression)
Provides efficient estimates
Valid inference (correct CIs and p-values)

Key Insight: For linear regression with normal errors, least squares = maximum likelihood

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Basic Interpretation Rules
Intercept (β₀): Mean Y at reference level of all variables
For continuous X: β₁ = change in mean Y for one-unit increase in X, holding all other variables constant
For categorical X: β₁ = difference in mean Y compared to reference level, holding all other variables constant

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Example: BMI Model
Interpretation: - BMI increased by 1.47 units from 1999-2000 to 2015-2016 - This is the SAME increase for all age/sex/race groups (additivity assumption)

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Coding Considerations
Continuous variables:

Is linearity appropriate?
What does zero mean? (Consider centering)
Should you scale? (e.g., age/10 for 10-year increments)

Categorical variables:

What is the reference level?
Should categories be combined?

Ordered categorical:

Code as continuous or unordered?
Risk of dichotomization?

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
What is Confounding?
Definition: Z is a confounder of X→Y association if:

Z affects X, AND
Z affects Y

Z (AGE) ↙ ↘ X Y
Key Problem: When X changes, Z also changes → difficult to isolate effect of X

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Example: Physical Exercise and BMI
Research question: Does physical exercise (PE) reduce BMI?
Unadjusted model: - PE coefficient: -2.15
Adjusted for age: - PE coefficient: -1.88
Interpretation: Part of the “effect” was due to younger people exercising more AND having lower BMI

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Controlling for Confounders
In regression models:

Include confounders as covariates
Interpretation becomes “holding Z constant”
Effect of X₂ is estimated comparing sub-populations that differ only in X₂

Important: This is NOT the same as establishing causality!
See Chapter 8 for causal inference methods

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
What is Effect Modification?
Definition: The association between X and Y differs across levels of Z
Also called:

Moderation
Interaction

Example: Does BMI increase over time differ by age group?

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Testing for Interaction
Two approaches:

Stratified analysis: Fit separate models for each level of Z

Inefficient
No formal test

Interaction term: Add X × Z to model

More efficient
Provides formal test

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Interaction Model
\[E(Y) = \beta_0 + \beta_1\text{YEAR} + \beta_2\text{AGE} + \beta_3(\text{AGE} \times \text{YEAR})\]
Interpretation:

Change in BMI for younger group: β₁
Change in BMI for older group: β₁ + β₃

Critical point: When interaction present, CANNOT interpret main effects alone!

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Example: Age-Year Interaction
Results:

Younger group: BMI increased 1.64 units
Older group: BMI increased 1.64 - 0.49 = 1.15 units
Interaction not significant (p = 0.3)

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Hypothesis Testing: Single Coefficient
Wald test: Tests H₀: β = 0
\[\text{Test statistic: } \frac{\hat{\beta}}{\text{SE}(\hat{\beta})}\]

Compare to normal distribution
Requires normality of estimates
Valid if Y is normal OR large sample

From output: P-value for each coefficient

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Hypothesis Testing: Multiple Coefficients
Likelihood Ratio Test: Compares nested models

Restricted model (M₀): Coefficients set to zero
Full model (M₁): Coefficients estimated
Tests if multiple βs are jointly different from zero

Example: Testing overall effect of RACE variable (4 coefficients)
Equivalent for linear regression: F-test comparing explained variance

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Comparing Non-Nested Models
Akaike Information Criterion (AIC): \[\text{AIC} = -2\log[L(M)] + 2k\]
Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC): \[\text{BIC} = -2\log[L(M)] + k\log(n)\]
Where: - L(M) = likelihood of model M - k = number of parameters - n = sample size
Interpretation: LOWER is better (BIC penalizes complexity more)

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Model Selection Strategy
Decision tree:

Pre-specified hypothesis? → Use conceptual model to select variables → Classical inference valid
Data-driven selection? → Use AIC/BIC for selection → Classical inference NOT valid → Focus on prediction

Key principle: Match objective → selection method → evaluation criteria

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Diagnostic Plots
1. QQ-plot: Check normality of residuals

Should show linear trend
Large samples: less critical

2. Residuals vs. Fitted: Check constant variance

Should show random scatter
Funnel shape → non-constant variance

3. Independence: Check study design

Repeated measures?
Clustering?

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
What to Do About Violations
Non-normality:

Less problematic with large n
May still affect inference

Non-constant variance:

More serious problem
Can invalidate tests
Consider transformations or robust SEs

Non-independence:

Very serious if ignored
Use appropriate methods (Chapter 9)
Mixed models, GEE, etc.

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
What Makes a “Good” Model?
Answer: Depends on your objective!

Hypothesis testing: Valid test assumptions
Explaining variability: High R² or R²ₐdⱼ
Causal inference: Control confounding + causal assumptions (Ch 8)
Prediction: High predictive accuracy

No single measure of overall adequacy

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
R² (Coefficient of Determination)
Definition: Proportion of variance in Y explained by X
\[R^2 = 1 - \frac{\text{Var}_{\text{res}}(M)}{\text{Var}(Y)}\]
Properties:

Always increases when adding variables
Use adjusted R² for model comparison
Low R² doesn’t mean bad model!

BMI example: R² = 4.8% - Age, sex, race, year explain ~5% of BMI variability - Typical for observational studies

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Predictive Accuracy
For prediction models:

Average squared prediction error
Critical: Test on NEW data (external validation)
Cross-validation to avoid overfitting

Warning signs of overfitting:

Too many predictors
Selected on same data being evaluated
Good internal, poor external validation

See Chapter 10 for predictive modeling

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Quantile Regression
Objective: Model percentiles instead of mean
Use cases:

Skewed outcomes
Interest in tails of distribution
Understanding variability changes

Example: Model 25th and 75th percentiles of BMI

Inter-quartile range as function of age
Different changes at different percentiles

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Non-Parametric Regression
Objective: Relax linearity assumption
Kernel smoothing:

Uniform kernel: Average Y in window around X
Normal kernel: Weighted average (closer = higher weight)

Limitation: Curse of dimensionality

Works well for 1-2 variables
Difficult with many covariates

Alternative: Generalized Additive Models (GAMs)

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Critical Concepts

Four objectives require different approaches and evaluation
Coefficient interpretation is conditional on other variables
Confounding is pervasive in observational studies
Interaction means main effects can’t be interpreted alone
Model assumptions matter differently for estimates vs. inference
“Good model” depends entirely on your objective

title: Lecture 8: Linear Regression Analysis
text:
Common Pitfalls
❌ Interpreting association as causation
❌ Ignoring confounders
❌ Hypothesis testing after data-driven selection
❌ Using R² alone to judge model quality
❌ Forgetting assumptions when doing inference

text:

A conceptual framework for health services utilization:


Conceptual models guide which factors to include/exclude in statistical models.

e.g.,) In examining hypotheses concerning the link between physical activity and health care costs,

but should not include mediating factors (such as BMI or self-reported health status: Need factors) in the statistical model.

Highly right-skewed

Example: Medical expenditures

Transformation approaches

title: Lecture 1: Introduction to Class

Goal: Learn patterns that optimize prediction accuracy

Focus on prediction, not mechanism
Minimize distance between observed and predicted outcomes
Often uses algorithmic “black box” methods

Less structured, fewer assumptions
Does not support causal inference

Purpose: Generate payment from payer for services

Only insured patients represented

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Learning Objectives
By the end of this session, you should be able to:

This chapter provides essential statistical foundations for analyzing healthcare data. Emphasize that healthcare outcomes rarely follow normal distributions, which motivates much of the material.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
MEPS Total Expenditure Example


Mean: $18,145
Median: $9,664
Extreme right skew with long tail
Mean > Median indicates right skewness


This is typical of healthcare expenditure data. A few high-cost users drive up the mean substantially above the median.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

Traditional “rule”: p < 0.05 = “statistically significant”

Large samples: Trivial effects can have tiny p-values

Small samples: Important effects may have large p-values

Low statistical power

Multiple comparisons: Error rate inflates

10 tests: P(at least 1 false positive) = 0.40

Solution: Pre-specify analysis plan, report all analyses conducted
Best practice: Focus on effect sizes and practical significance

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:

Example: Testing 10 covariates individually for association with expenditures

Each test at α = 0.05

Bonferroni correction: Test each at α/k level
False discovery rate: Control proportion of false positives
Pre-specification: Develop strong conceptual model first

text:

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Populations and Samples
Population: The complete group we want to learn about

Well-defined (e.g., all Hiroshima atomic bomb survivors who survived 1+ years)
Can be hypothetical (e.g., all breast cancer patients who have/will undergo mastectomy)

Sample: A subset of the population used for inference

Random samples enable quantification of uncertainty
Many healthcare studies use convenience samples or complete censuses

Sub-population: A population subset satisfying specific criteria

Defined by fixed characteristics (e.g., men under 20 in Hiroshima cohort)
Regression models estimate means for sub-populations defined by covariates


Emphasize that representativeness is always a concern, regardless of how samples are obtained. Discuss how this relates to external validity.

text:
Random Variables in Healthcare
Healthcare outcomes are random variables that vary across individuals:

Binary: Re-admission after surgery (Yes/No)
Categorical: Treatment type (surgery/radiation/hormonal)
Count: Number of outpatient visits, prescriptions filled
Continuous: Medical expenditures, length of stay

Notation: - Capital letters (X, Y) for generic/theoretical variables - Lowercase letters (x, y) for specific observed values

Give concrete examples from students’ experience. Ask: What healthcare outcomes have they encountered? What types of variables are these?

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Dependent vs. Independent Variables
Research Question Determines the Relationship

Dependent variable (Y): Outcome or response
Independent variable (X): Predictor or covariate

Example: Exercise and insomnia

Exercise may reduce insomnia → Exercise is X, insomnia is Y
Insomnia may reduce exercise ability → Insomnia is X, exercise is Y
Both may be true (feedback loop) → Modeling challenge!

Key principle: Variables that co-evolve should often both be considered outcomes

Discuss the importance of conceptual models (like Andersen-Newman) in sorting out variable relationships. Medical expenditures and hospitalizations example from the text.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Statistical Distributions
A distribution describes the probability that a variable takes any value in its range
For categorical variables: Finite set of probabilities (sum to 1)
For continuous variables: Probability density function (PDF)

Area under PDF over an interval = probability of value in that interval
Cumulative distribution function (CDF) = probability ≤ specified value

Key summaries: - Mean (expected value): Most typical value, influenced by extremes - Median (50th percentile): Center of distribution, robust to outliers

Healthcare data is often right-skewed, so median may be more representative than mean. Show the MEPS expenditure histogram from Figure 2.1.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Parameters and Models
Parameters: Greek letters (μ, σ, α, β) that specify a distribution

Normal distribution: mean μ, variance σ²
Parametric methods: specify family, estimate parameters

Models: Assumptions and mathematical specifications for analysis

Rarely unique - multiple models may address same question
Model choice affects both estimates and their standard errors
What constitutes a “good model” is a recurring theme


Emphasize that model assumptions matter greatly. Healthcare outcomes often violate normality assumption, motivating specialized distributions.

title: Lecture 2: Key Statistical Concepts
text:
Estimation and Inference
Estimation: Using sample data to learn about population

Sample mean estimates population mean
Sample median estimates population median

Statistical Inference: Using estimates to answer research questions

Combines estimates with their uncertainty (standard errors)
Hypothesis tests are one tool for inference

Standard Error (SE): Quantifies variation over repeated samples

Higher SE → greater expected variation
Decreases with larger sample size
Depends on the model used


Different models can yield similar point estimates but very different standard errors, affecting inference. Preview the two-part model discussion from Chapter 6.

Rich information on healthcare utilization

Research value despite not designed for research
